Two-syllable words always carry the stress on the fist syllable. For three-syllable words, stress on the penultimate syllable contrasts with stress on the first syllable as follows: kokára 'type of ritual' sisíya 'talking' wagúra 'craw-fish sp.' kókara 'fish sp.' sísiya 'ants' wágura 'yam sp.' ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Disyllables are stressed on the first syllable; in trisyllables stress is lexically either initial or penultimate (minimal pairs exist), so stress is contrastive only in three-syllable words; the source calls stress otherwise 'predictable' but gives no explicit rule for words of four or more syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Three-syllable words are the stated exception to predictability (initial vs penultimate contrast: kokára/kókara, sisíya/sísiya, wagúra/wágura). Evensen 1993:14 adds that the penultimate-stressed trisyllabic class selects the locative clitic allomorph /-i.ya/ (tawáiya 'in his house' vs watéya 'in his place').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms (isolated lexical items with acute marks); no statement about phrase-level prominence. 4-page draft OPD 'posted as is without peer review'; the fuller primary analysis is the unpublished Evensen & Evensen 1982 phonemes ms.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD is titled 'Umanakaina (Gwedena) Language [GDN]', Bonenepi village, Rabaraba, Milne Bay Province; Evensen 1993 states the analysis is based on the 'Main Dialect' as defined in Jesudason & Jesudason 1991 dialect survey. Dutton 1975:643 notes two dialects of Gwedena (upper Ugu vs. the rest) and equates Gwedena with Capell's 'Umanakaina'. Same languoid as uman1240; no separate dialect glottocode needed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Disyllables are always stressed on the first syllable; in trisyllables stress is lexically contrastive between the first and the penultimate (second) syllable (minimal pairs kokára/kókara, sisíya/sísiya, wagúra/wágura); the OPD says nothing about longer words. Evensen 1993 independently treats 'three-syllable words with penultimate stress' as a lexical class that selects the /-iya/ allomorph of the person-specific location clitic (e.g. tawa 'house' -> ta.wai.ya 'in his house' vs wata 'place' -> wa.te.ya 'in his place'), which confirms that penultimate stress in trisyllables is a word-specific property rather than a rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the trisyllabic contrast itself; the OPD calls stress predictable everywhere except three-syllable words. The stressed-vowel marks in the Evensen 1993 examples (p.15-16) did not survive scanned, so the individual marked forms are not quoted.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD is labelled 'Umanakaina (Gwedena) Language [GDN], Rabaraba, Milne Bay Province', main village Bonenepi. Evensen 1993 states its analysis 'is based on data from the Main Dialect of the language as defined . "A Dialect Survey Report On The Umanakaina Language Area", by Daniel & Wei Lei Jesudason, January 1991' (p.1). Dutton 1975 p.643 notes two Gwedena dialects (upper Ugu vs the rest of the area) and identifies Gwedena with Capell's 'Umanakaina'.
